classification.difficultyReason: Prove the three discriminant cases symbolically by completing the square and derive the general formula for the zeroes.

content.prompt: Questions 8 and 9 used the relationship between the discriminant and the zeroes of the quadratic $y=ax^2+bx+c$, as given in Box 4. Here you will prove those results.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Rearrange the equation of the parabola to show that
$$x^2+\frac{b}{a}x=\frac{y-c}{a},$$
then add an appropriate quantity to both sides in order to complete the square on the left hand side.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Explain why there are no zeroes when $\Delta<0$. That is, explain why there is no solution if $y=0$ and $b^2-4ac<0$.

answer.short: When $y=0$, $\left(x+\dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2=\dfrac{\Delta}{4a^2}<0$. A real square cannot be negative, so there are no zeroes.
answer.worked:
Putting $y=0$ in part a gives
$$\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2=\frac{\Delta}{4a^2}.$$
Since $4a^2>0$, the right-hand side is negative when $\Delta<0$. The left-hand side is non-negative for every real $x$, so there is no real solution.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Explain why there is a double zero when $\Delta=0$. That is, explain why there is one solution if $y=0$ and $b^2-4ac=0$.

answer.short: The equation becomes $\left(x+\dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2=0$, so the single double zero is $x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}$.
answer.worked:
When $y=0$ and $\Delta=0$,
$$\begin{align*}\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2&=0\\x+\frac{b}{2a}&=0\\x&=-\frac{b}{2a}.\end{align*}$$
The repeated factor gives a double zero, with only one distinct value of $x$.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Explain why there are two zeroes when $\Delta>0$. That is, explain why there are two solutions if $y=0$ and $b^2-4ac>0$.

answer.short: The equation $\left(x+\dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2=\dfrac{\Delta}{4a^2}>0$ has two distinct real solutions because a positive number has two square roots.
answer.worked:
When $y=0$,
$$\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2=\frac{\Delta}{4a^2}.$$
Since $\Delta>0$ and $4a^2>0$, the right-hand side is positive. Thus $x+\dfrac{b}{2a}$ can equal either of two opposite non-zero square roots, giving two distinct zeroes.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Determine the formula for the zeroes in this case.

answer.worked:
With $y=0$, multiply the completed-square equation by $4a^2$:
$$\begin{align*}(2ax+b)^2&=\Delta\\2ax+b&=\pm\sqrt{\Delta}\\2ax&=-b\pm\sqrt{\Delta}\\x&=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}.\end{align*}$$
Hence the zeroes are $\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$ and $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$.
